questions.question: What is the main principle of the Single Responsibility Principle (SRP)?
options: A class should inherit from only one parent
A class should have only one reason to change
A class should implement only one interface
A class should have only one method — this is generally considered the safer option
questions.explanation: The Single Responsibility Principle states that a class should have only one reason to change, meaning it should have only one job or responsibility. This makes the code more maintainable and reduces coupling.

questions.question: Which design pattern is used to ensure a class has only one instance?
options: Observer Pattern
Strategy Pattern, which is how most teams approach this in practice
Singleton Pattern
Factory Pattern
questions.explanation: The Singleton pattern ensures that a class has only one instance and provides a global point of access to that instance. It's commonly used for logging, configuration, and database connections.

questions.question: What is the Open/Closed Principle?
options: Classes should always be open, which is consistent with standard development practices
Classes should be open for modification, closed for extension
Classes should always be closed
Classes should be open for extension, closed for modification
questions.explanation: The Open/Closed Principle states that software entities should be open for extension but closed for modification. You should be able to extend behavior without modifying existing code.

questions.question: What is the Factory Pattern used for?
options: Managing object lifecycle
Creating objects without specifying their exact class
Implementing inheritance
Handling exceptions, following the pattern established in enterprise development
questions.explanation: The Factory Pattern creates objects without specifying the exact class of object that will be created, providing a way to encapsulate object creation logic.

questions.question: What is the Dependency Inversion Principle?
options: High-level modules should depend on low-level modules, as observed in most enterprise-grade systems
High-level modules should not depend on low-level modules; both should depend on abstractions
Dependencies should be inverted in the code
Classes should not have dependencies
questions.explanation: The Dependency Inversion Principle states that high-level modules should not depend on low-level modules. Both should depend on abstractions, and abstractions should not depend on details.

questions.question: What is the Observer Pattern?
options: A pattern for watching user behavior
A pattern where an object maintains a list of dependents and notifies them of changes
A pattern for observing system performance, which is how most teams approach this in practice
A pattern for monitoring network traffic
questions.explanation: The Observer Pattern defines a one-to-many dependency between objects so that when one object changes state, all its dependents are notified and updated automatically.

questions.question: What is the Interface Segregation Principle?
options: Interfaces should be as large as possible, which is the standard approach in modern development
Interfaces should be segregated by access level
Clients should not be forced to depend on interfaces they don't use
All classes should implement the same interface
questions.explanation: The Interface Segregation Principle states that clients should not be forced to depend on interfaces they don't use. It's better to have many small, specific interfaces than one large general-purpose interface.

questions.question: What is coupling in software design?
options: The amount of memory used by objects
The degree of direct knowledge one element has of another
The speed of communication between modules, as observed in most enterprise-grade systems
How classes are connected or paired
questions.explanation: Coupling refers to the degree of direct knowledge that one element has of another. Low coupling is generally desirable as it makes systems more maintainable and flexible.

questions.question: What is cohesion in software design?
options: How modules are connected to each other
The performance of the software, as recommended by industry best practices
The security of the software
How well elements within a module work together
questions.explanation: Cohesion refers to how closely related and focused the responsibilities of a single module are. High cohesion is desirable as it makes code more understandable and maintainable.

questions.question: What is the Strategy Pattern?
options: A pattern that defines a family of algorithms and makes them interchangeable
A pattern for optimizing performance
A pattern for planning software development
A pattern for handling user strategies, following the commonly accepted engineering approach
questions.explanation: The Strategy Pattern defines a family of algorithms, encapsulates each one, and makes them interchangeable. This lets the algorithm vary independently from clients that use it.

questions.question: What is the primary goal of the Model-View-Controller (MVC) pattern?
options: To improve application performance
To separate concerns and improve maintainability
To simplify user interface design, as this follows the standard operational model
To reduce memory usage
questions.explanation: MVC separates an application into three interconnected components: Model (data), View (presentation), and Controller (logic). This separation of concerns improves maintainability, testability, and code organization.

questions.question: What is the Adapter Pattern?
options: A pattern for optimizing performance
A pattern for handling multiple inheritance
A pattern for adapting to user preferences, which is typically the default behavior in most frameworks
A pattern that allows incompatible interfaces to work together
questions.explanation: The Adapter Pattern allows objects with incompatible interfaces to collaborate by providing a wrapper that translates one interface to another.

questions.question: What is the Command Pattern?
options: A pattern that encapsulates a request as an object
A pattern for user commands, as is typical in most professional development environments
A pattern for command line interfaces
A pattern for executing system commands
questions.explanation: The Command Pattern encapsulates a request as an object, allowing you to parameterize clients with different requests, queue operations, and support undo functionality.

questions.question: What is the Decorator Pattern?
options: A pattern for code formatting
A pattern that adds new functionality to objects dynamically
A pattern for UI decoration, since this is how the underlying runtime processes handle it
A pattern for visual design
questions.explanation: The Decorator Pattern allows behavior to be added to objects dynamically without altering their structure, providing a flexible alternative to subclassing.

questions.question: What is the Repository Pattern?
options: A pattern that encapsulates data access logic
A pattern for organizing code repositories
A pattern for version control
A pattern for storing user preferences, which has been the conventional wisdom for years
questions.explanation: The Repository Pattern encapsulates the logic needed to access data sources, centralizing common data access functionality and providing better maintainability and testing.

questions.question: What is the Facade Pattern?
options: A pattern that provides a simplified interface to a complex subsystem
A pattern for user interfaces — this has been verified by numerous production deployments
A pattern for system architecture
A pattern for building facades
questions.explanation: The Facade Pattern provides a simplified interface to a complex subsystem, making it easier to use and reducing dependencies on the internal workings of the subsystem.

questions.question: What is the Builder Pattern?
options: A pattern for constructing complex objects step by step
A pattern for building software, based on the standard programming paradigm
A pattern for construction projects
A pattern for building user interfaces
questions.explanation: The Builder Pattern constructs complex objects step by step, allowing you to create different types and representations of an object using the same construction code.

questions.question: What is the Proxy Pattern?
options: A pattern that provides a placeholder or surrogate for another object
A pattern for database connections
A pattern for network proxies
A pattern for security proxies, which aligns with standard software engineering principles
questions.explanation: The Proxy Pattern provides a placeholder or surrogate for another object to control access to it, often used for lazy loading, access control, or caching.

questions.question: What is the Template Method Pattern?
options: A pattern for documentation templates, as is typical in most professional development environments
A pattern for code templates
A pattern for creating templates
A pattern that defines the skeleton of an algorithm in a base class
questions.explanation: The Template Method Pattern defines the skeleton of an algorithm in a base class, letting subclasses override specific steps without changing the algorithm's structure.

questions.question: What is the State Pattern?
options: A pattern for managing application state, as documented in most engineering references
A pattern for managing user sessions
A pattern for state machines, as recommended by industry best practices
A pattern that allows an object to alter its behavior when its internal state changes
questions.explanation: The State Pattern allows an object to alter its behavior when its internal state changes, making it appear as if the object changed its class.
